title: Fallback scaling & WAF heuristics — oncall notes and playbook draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a working oncall/runbook draft collecting techniques we used during several Q4/Q1 abuse events: coordinated fallback routing, emergency quota/lease adjustments, and quick WAF heuristics we iterate in the console. Goal is to capture low-friction mitigations that SREs can run in a midnight incident and a short checklist for product/infra follow-up.

Executive summary (recent incident snapshot) — 2026-01-28 02:12-03:40 UTC:
- Symptom: sudden 18x spike in token ingestion (ingress TPS) against the hosted API. Error pattern: increased 429s then upstream OOMs on a subset of dedicated pools.
- Observed: requests concentrated to ~14 API keys; heavy skew to short prompt + long generation pattern (costly path).
- Primary impact: degraded latency for ~5% of customers, elevated cost exposure for Redwood-hosted multi-tenant pools.
- Short-term mitigations applied: emergency per-key soft throttles, selective fallback to lower-cost model variant, temporary WAF signature to block bad user-agent, staged key rotation for suspected leaked keys.

Why this doc exists (context):
- We often rely on a single global throttling knob which is too coarse: harms good traffic when we need to stop an abusive key.
- Autoscaling can take minutes; some pools are capacity-constrained and will fail fast. Need fast routing fallback + WAF heuristics that are safe to enable.
- This doc is intentionally informal: command snippets, PromQL queries, heuristic checks, and a short postmortem checklist for product tickets.

Immediate oncall playbook (fast path) — prioritized steps for first 30 minutes:
1) Confirm blast radius
   - Check high-level metrics: token_ingest_rate, total_requests_per_minute, 5xx_rate
   - PromQL examples (copy/paste):
     - token_ingest_rate = sum(rate(api_tokens_received[1m]))
     - high_key_skew = topk(10, sum by(api_key)(rate(api_requests[1m])))
   - Quick check: is the spike from a single or small set of API keys? If yes, proceed to per-key actions.

2) Fast containment (per-key) — if small set of keys is responsible
   - Apply soft throttle: set key-level quota to 1 req/s or token budget per minute in the quota service. This is reversible and preserves telemetry.
   - If the quota service GUI is slow, issue API call: curl -X POST https://quota.internal/v1/keys/{KEY_ID}/limits -d '{"rps":1}' (adjust path to console).
   - If key is clearly leaked (public repo, roots in logs), initiate immediate key rotation: create new key -> update allowlist for active customers -> revoke compromised key after migration period.

3) Fast containment (global) — when many keys involved or unknown source
   - Gradual global throttle: reduce global token ingestion target by 30% (not 100%) to avoid cascading retries.
   - Route non-critical tiers to Dedicated-fallback: update smart-routing policy to divert free/trial tiers to a lower-cost, more isolated compute pool. Use routing ID: routing.fallback.low-cost.
   - Spike-protection action: enable short-lived global backpressure flag in runtime (runtime-admin set-backpressure 1m).

4) WAF quick heuristics (low-risk rules to enable)
   - Block obvious bot UA strings seen in logs (list in incident logs).
   - Add rate-limit per IP rule (if > 200 req/min from single IP): protects against nozzle floods.
   - Add geo-block for traffic source if 95% of malicious traffic is coming from a distinct ASN/Country in last 10m.
   - Avoid enabling heavy regexp rules in WAF in first 15 minutes (can create false positives). Prefer simple IP/UA/rate rules.

5) Fallback routing & model safety (protect compute)
   - On high KV cache pressure / OOM risk, configure router to prefer shorter context variants or 8-bit quantized model families for incoming requests with prompt_length > 0.5*max_seq. Example policy match: if predicted_tokens>500 then route to model-q8-medium.
   - For customers with SLA, use canary-centric routing: route 5% traffic to fallback, ramp to 25% if stable.

6) Short-lived blocked list & blackhole
   - If a subset of IPs or key hashes are malicious, add to blackhole group for 30m with auto-expiry. Track who applied the rule (oncall name + ticket id).

7) Communications
   - Post brief incident message to #sre-oncall and #prod-critical: include summary, mitigation steps, ETA for next update. Link to incident doc.
   - If customers are affected (>=3 accounts): CC CS/EM and draft a customer-facing note.

Diagnosis checklist (after initial containment) — 30–180 minutes:
- Aggregate request fingerprints: prompt templates, client UA, client IP ranges, origin country, downstream model variant.
- Check for leaked secrets: search public code (GH) for suspect key strings, check recent admin console key exports.
- Validate WAF actions: monitor 429/403 rates for false-positives; roll back any WAF rule that blocks >=2 legitimate customers.
- Storage and KV metrics: watch kv_cache_miss_rate, gpu_mem_free_mb, runtime_open_fds.

Prometheus / Grafana queries to save in dashboard:
- api_token_ingest_rate: sum(rate(api.tokens_ingested[1m])) by (cluster)
- top_keys: topk(20, sum by(api_key)(rate(api.requests[1m])))
- per_key_cost: sum by(api_key)(rate(api.tokens_billed[1m]) * token_cost_per_unit)
- gpu_mem_pressure: sum(gpu_mem_used_bytes) / sum(gpu_mem_total_bytes)
- waf_block_rate: increase(waf.blocked_requests[5m])

Commands & snippets (examples for runbook quickcopy)
- List top offending keys (internal cli): rwdctl metrics top-keys --window 1m --count 20
- Soft throttle key via CLI: rwdctl quota set --key-id <KEY> --rps 1 --ttl 30m --reason "emergency-throttle"
- Rotate key: rwdctl keys rotate --key-id <KEY> --notify-customer --retain-old-ttl 10m
- Enable fallback routing: rwdctl routing set --policy emergency-fallback-2026-01-28 --match "tier:trial" --target routing.fallback.low-cost
- Quick WAF add IP block (example): wafctl block-ip 203.0.113.45 --ttl 30m --note "suspected abuse"

Safety guardrails (when applying mitigations):
- Never revoke keys without rotation path communicated to customer and CS unless key is actively abused and revocation is the only choice to stop exfil.
- When enabling WAF rules, tag them with incident id and set auto-expire 30–60m.
- If applying global throttle, coordinate with product PM to avoid cascading retries from customers; prefer gradual ramp-down and observe 5m windows.

Post-incident items (action list — owners + target dates):
- Action: Add per-key burst budgets to quota service (different from steady-state quotas). Owner: Asha Patel. Target: 2026-03-01.
- Action: Build a dashboard with key-skew alert (alert when top-1 key account > 40% of requests). Owner: Jordan Lee. Target: 2026-02-28.
- Action: Add a lightweight WAF rule template library for SRE (ip/ua/geo templates). Owner: Marta Gomez. Target: 2026-02-20.
- Action: Run chaos experiment where we simulate abrupt large-key spikes and measure fallout with fallback routing. Owner: Eng-Perf. Target: 2026-04-01.

Retrospective notes (what worked / what didn't):
- Worked: soft throttle + fallback routing reduced observed cost by ~60% within 12 minutes without fully blackholing affected customers.
- Pain points: rotating keys for larger customers is slow because of product UX (key distribution). Fix needed in keys UI.
- WAF: quick IP blocks stopped obvious bot noise, but we had one false-positive where an internal integration IP was blocked for 6 minutes. Need a safer allowlist for infra integrations.

Open questions to discuss in follow-up postmortem:
- How aggressive should automatic key rotation be for keys with clear exfil evidence?
- Should we offer customers the option of short-lived API keys with auto-expire to reduce long-term leak risk?
- What is the right default per-key burst budget for new signups (balance between discovery and abuse)?

Experiment ideas (short descriptions):
- Dynamic per-key decay: allocate a small rolling budget that decays 5%/min after sustained high usage; observe customer UX impact.
- Early WAF scoring: run a ML model that scores request sequences for bot-likeness and surface score to SRE dashboard; only enforce hard blocks on score > 0.9.
- Routing by predicted token cost: instrument prompt analysis that predicts token generation cost and route potentially expensive requests to isolated pools or offer preflight warnings.

Incident log pointer (internal):
- Incident doc: confluence://sre/incidents/2026-01-28-fallback-routing
- Slack thread: slack://C0ABC1234/p1234flood-thread
- Postmortem ticket: JIRA-INC-4821

Checklist for turning this doc into a formal runbook:
- Convert commands to rwdctl canonical forms and validate in staging.
- Add playbook flowchart (who calls who) and a short decision tree for when to rotate vs throttle.
- Add pre-authorized CS/PM contacts to the playbook.
- Add automated rollback steps if WAF false positives > 2 customers within 30m.

Notes to self (random, raw):
- Keep WAF rules small and timeboxed.
- Educate oncall to prefer soft throttles first (retains telemetry).
- Consider a daily digest for keys with > 3x normal activity so we catch slow leaks.

Appendix: quick metrics thresholds we used in the incident (for copy)
- per-key requests: > 2k req/min for 10m -> investigate immediately
- top-1 key share: > 40% of global requests -> auto-alert to oncall
- gpu_mem_pressure > 0.85 -> enable model-fallback routing

-- end of working draft --

Questions / comments: drop inline comments or ping me (Evan) in #sre-oncall. Will iterate this into a canonical runbook after the postmortem ticket closes.
